keyVerseText: And ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God: it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun קָלִי (qâlîy) derives from the root קָלָה (qâlâh), which carries the sense of roasting, parching, or drying by heat. This root emphasizes a process of toasting or scorching that transforms grain into a preserved, edible form. Thus, beyond the simple idea of 'parched corn,' the root conveys the intentional preparation of grain through fire, highlighting a stage of transformation and readiness for consumption.
usageInScripture: The word qâlîy appears six times in Scripture, consistently referring to parched or roasted grain, often described as a common food. Translations such as 'and parched,' 'nor parched corn,' and 'her parched' illustrate the term's consistent association with grain that has been dried or roasted for eating. This usage underscores its role as a staple sustenance in ancient Israelite life, reflecting both practical nourishment and ritual significance.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding qâlîy as parched grain prepared by roasting enriches our grasp of biblical imagery related to provision and God's care for His people. The preparation of grain through fire can symbolize purification and readiness, themes echoed throughout Scripture in God's refining work. Moreover, as a common food, qâlîy reminds believers of the ordinary means through which God sustains life, pointing ultimately to Christ as the Bread of Life who nourishes spiritually. Recognizing the word's rootedness in physical sustenance invites reflection on God's faithful provision in both body and soul.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 23:14 commands that neither bread nor parched corn (קָלִי) nor green ears are to be eaten until an offering is made to God, establishing a perpetual statute. The inclusion of qâlîy here highlights the sanctity of even the most basic forms of sustenance, emphasizing that all provision is to be acknowledged as coming from God. This underscores the importance of honoring God first in all things, including daily nourishment, reinforcing a posture of dependence and gratitude.
